headline: Carta and NewView Team Up to Monetize Employee Desperation
subheadline: Two companies that profit from illiquidity announce a partnership to make illiquidity slightly less painful—for a fee.
source_headline: Carta and NewView partner, hoping to entice more startups to let employees sell shares early
body_html:
Carta, the cap table software company that has quietly become the plumbing beneath cap tables everywhere, is partnering with NewView to create what both companies are calling a solution to employee liquidity constraints. The partnership aims to make tender offers—the process by which private company employees can sell their shares before an IPO or acquisition—easier to execute and more accessible to startups. This is, according to the companies involved, a gift to the working people who have been locked into illiquid equity packages for years while their employers burned cash and promised exits. The cynical observer might notice that making tender offers easier also makes tender offers more frequent, and more frequent tender offers generate more transaction fees for the intermediaries running the show.

Carta has built an extraordinary business by owning the critical infrastructure that tracks who owns what in private companies. Founders, investors, and employees all depend on Carta's software to understand their cap tables—a dependency that has made Carta indispensable and profitable without ever needing to prove a particularly compelling business model beyond "we are the only people who do this." NewView, meanwhile, has positioned itself as a facilitator of secondary transactions in private company equity, matching employees who want to sell with investors who want to buy. Together, they are announcing that they will remove friction from the tender offer process, which sounds humanitarian until you realize that friction is what has been protecting everyone's sanity by preventing constant market-making in shares that nobody can actually value accurately.

This partnership is not new thinking. Both companies have obvious financial incentives to increase transaction volume—more deals mean more fees, more data, more entrenchment. Carta already occupies such a central position in private company infrastructure that it can afford to be patient about monetization; NewView needs secondary deals to justify its existence and attract capital. The announcement is essentially two toll collectors declaring that they have found a way to make the toll roads prettier so more cars will use them, which is great for toll collection but may not be great for the cars.

The companies have dressed this up in the language of "opportunity" and "access." Startups, they explain, will be "encouraged" to allow employees to cash out early through easier mechanics. One might translate this as: "We have built tools that make it frictionless for startups to execute tender offers, which means founders will feel social pressure to run them, which means employees will believe they can finally get some value out of their equity grants, which means everyone will use our platform, and we will collect fees on both sides of these transactions." There is nothing illegal about this, and there is nothing particularly wrong with it either—except that it profits most from the moment when employees are most desperate, which is when they need the money most urgently.

What could go wrong? The most obvious risk is price discovery. In illiquid markets with asymmetric information, tender offers tend to price shares at levels that please neither buyer nor seller. Employees, starved for liquidity, often take discounts to what shares might be worth at exit. Investors, meanwhile, get data about how desperate employees are feeling, which becomes a signal about company health. If tender offers become routine, startups might find themselves constantly running internal secondaries that drain morale without actually solving the underlying problem: that private companies take too long to exit, and employees should probably be getting paid in cash.

The broader pattern here is unmistakable. The VC ecosystem has created a problem—illiquidity—and every actor within it has an incentive to profit from managing that problem rather than solving it. Equity compensation exists because companies cannot afford to pay cash. Tender offers exist because employees cannot wait for exits. Secondary markets exist because both of these truths are permanent features of private company life. Now platforms exist to make secondary markets efficient, which means the ecosystem has successfully monetized its own structural dysfunction. This is not a conspiracy; it is just incentives aligned in the direction of extracting value from the gap between promise and reality.

Carta and NewView are not doing anything wrong. They are simply ensuring that every person involved in private company equity—founder, investor, employee, and intermediary—pays a small price to move their shares one inch closer to actual value. It is the most VC thing possible: identify a problem created by the system, build infrastructure to manage it, then profit from the management. The employees will feel relieved that they can finally unlock some value. Carta and NewView will feel relieved that they have found a new revenue stream. And private companies will continue burning cash while their employees wait, just a little bit less uncomfortably, for the exit that keeps getting pushed back.
glossary_definition: A ceremony in which a private company allows employees to sell shares back to the company or investors, creating the appearance of progress toward liquidity while actually confirming that the IPO is still years away.
